title: Anthropic Just Minted 5,000 Millionaires. Now What?
summary: What happens when AI engineers become multimillionaires overnight? Anthropic's IPO raises difficult questions about retention, startups, and stock dilution.
body_markdown:
*What happens when AI engineers become multimillionaires overnight? Anthropic's IPO raises difficult questions about retention, startups, and stock dilution.*


***KEY TAKEAWAYS***


-


Anthropic completed the largest IPO in history. The company raised approximately $81.3 billion at $83 per share, and its stock closed its first trading session at $97.17, giving it a market capitalization of roughly $1.27 trillion.


-


The IPO created extraordinary employee wealth. Anthropic's approximately 5,300 employees collectively held an estimated $232 billion in stock at the offering price, with roughly 96% reportedly holding stakes worth more than $1 million.


-


The local economic impact of IPO wealth may be smaller than expected. Research examining more than 700 California IPOs found that nearby home prices increased approximately 0.7% to 0.9%, with much of the effect occurring around the offering rather than after insider selling restrictions expired.


-


Research links successful IPOs to increased startup formation. Federal Reserve economists found that the increase in employee departures following successful IPOs was concentrated among workers leaving to join or establish startups, particularly higher-paid employees.


-


Anthropic faces potential employee retention and shareholder dilution challenges. Employees could sell only a limited portion of their holdings immediately, while the difference between the company's $1.27 trillion current-share valuation and $1.76 trillion fully diluted valuation highlights the significance of outstanding equity claims.


***MY HOT TAKES***


-


Anthropic's greatest competitive threat may be the people it just made rich. When hundreds of brilliant engineers suddenly have the financial independence to pursue their own ideas, keeping them becomes a much more complicated proposition.


-


The real trickle-down effect isn't luxury real estate—it's entrepreneurship. The most important economic consequence of Anthropic's IPO may be the companies that haven't been founded yet, created by employees who can finally afford to take extraordinary risks.


-


Investors celebrating Anthropic's market capitalization should pay closer attention to its fully diluted share count. Stock compensation may be necessary to retain talent, but every additional share potentially reduces existing shareholders' ownership.


-


Lockup expirations deserve more attention than first-day trading volume. The real test of investor demand comes when employees and early shareholders gain the freedom to convert substantial paper wealth into cash.


-


Anthropic's IPO could be fantastic for the AI ecosystem and considerably less fantastic for its shareholders. The same wealth creation that finances the next generation of AI startups may ultimately create the competitors that challenge Anthropic's extraordinary valuation.


-


You can quote me: *"Anthropic’s most valuable asset rides the elevator down to the lobby every night–and as of yesterday, most of that asset can afford not to come back up."*


***See you Monday.*** Back in the day–way back–when I first started on Wall Street, there was a trading floor lottery pool, and there was always that guy. You know the one. We would each stuff five dollars into an envelope whenever the jackpot got big enough to make the evening news, and somewhere between the collection and the drawing he would announce–to nobody in particular–that the money would not change him. He loved the work. He loved the team. He would be at his desk Monday morning, same as always. And every single one of us nodded politely and thought the exact same thing. No, you won’t. 🤣 Nobody ever believed that guy. Not his coworkers, not his boss, and certainly not his wife. We never had to find out, of course, because we never hit, LOL. Yesterday, roughly 5,000 people did–all at the same company, all on the same morning. And Wall Street just made a very large bet that every one of them will be at their desk on Monday. Hold that thought.


In case you missed it, but I know you didn’t, Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq yesterday under the ticker ANT. You have seen the headlines, so I will be quick. The deal priced Wednesday night at $83 a share, above a range that had been $70 to $78. The company and its founders sold about 980 million shares and raised $81.3 billion–billion, with a ‘B’–making it the largest IPO in history and knocking SpaceX off a perch it held for all of five months. The stock opened at $111.50, some 34% above the offering price, and closed at $97.17–up 17% on a day when the broader market was selling off. At that close the company is worth roughly $1.27 trillion based on the shares that exist today, or roughly $1.76 trillion if you count every share and option that could exist someday (fully diluted, for those keeping score).


But the number that caught my eye is not on the ticker. Anthropic had about 5,300 employees as of September. At the $83 offering price, the stock those employees hold was worth approximately $232 billion. Divide one by the other and you get about $44 million per person–PER PERSON–and that is at the offering price, not the close. One firm that tracks private-company shares estimates that roughly 96% of the staff is now sitting on more than $1 million, about 2,800 of them on more than $10 million, and around 600 on more than $100 million. The company is five years old. Go on, read that again. 👀


Naturally, everybody within fifty miles of San Francisco is busy spending that money on the employees’ behalf. Redfin calculates that current and former Anthropic workers now have enough wealth to buy 9% of all the homes in the city. All seven founders have pledged to give 80% of their stock to philanthropy, and the company matches a portion of what employees pledge, so the charities are circling. So is Sacramento, which collected an estimated $1.3 billion in taxes from Facebook’s IPO back in 2012–a deal that looks like a rounding error next to this one. Realtors, car dealers, private schools, the taxman. This is the trickle-down story, and you are going to hear it all weekend.


UM...not so fast. Somebody actually studied this. Researchers looked at more than 700 California IPOs between 1993 and 2017 and measured what happened to home prices near each company’s headquarters. The answer? They rose by somewhere between 0.7% and 0.9%. Not 9%. Let's call it: less than one. And here is the part I love–the bump showed up around the filing and the offering itself, NOT later when insiders were finally free to sell. People spend the money before they have it. Indeed, some Anthropic employees reportedly pledged shares to buy homes months ago. Meanwhile, the City of San Francisco cannot levy an income tax, so it will not see a direct dime of this windfall, and California’s own budget analyst spent this week warning that booms like this one have a habit of ending abruptly. The trickle is real. It is just more of a trickle than a flood.


So where does IPO money really go? History has an answer, and it is not granite countertops. Microsoft went public in 1986, and by one widely cited estimate it had minted roughly 10,000 millionaires by the year 2000. Google went public in 2004 and created at least 900 instant millionaires out of about 2,300 employees–including, famously, the company chef and the masseuse. The chef was gone within a year, off to go into business for himself with Google stock as his seed money. Facebook went public in May of 2012, and within weeks its chief technology officer announced he was leaving to start his own company while the tech press braced for a wave of exits. Notice a pattern? The newly rich do not all buy a boat and disappear. A good many of them walk out the door and build something.


The data backs it up. Economists at the Federal Reserve, working with Census records, found that a successful IPO increases the number of employees who leave–and that the entire increase comes from people leaving for STARTUPS, not for established competitors. It is also the highest-paid people who go. In other words, the IPO does not just make employees rich. It makes them brave. I watched a version of this in the late 1990s, when it seemed like every Friday brought another goodbye cake and another colleague off to a startup. A University of Florida academic, who has studied IPOs for decades, put it plainly this week: going public typically brings an increase in turnover. And you do not have to take a professor’s word for it. Anthropic said so itself–its prospectus lists holding on to its founders and key technical people among the risks to the business.


Now, to be fair, there is no exodus. Not yet, anyway. The same firm that counted all those millionaires says the company has seen very little attrition, and why would it? Employees were permitted to sell only up to 10% of their holdings on day one–as many as 315 million shares–with the rest released in stages through the middle of next May. Much of their stock has not vested at all. And by all accounts these are true believers who are convinced they are working on the most important technology of their lifetimes. Nobody quits the Friday after the drawing. The interesting question is who is still there after the last check clears.


Here is why this matters to you as an investor, even if you never plan to own a single share of ANT. This company has no oil wells and no patents on a blockbuster drug. Its most valuable asset rides the elevator down to the lobby every night–and as of yesterday, most of that asset can afford not to come back up. How do you keep a person who already has $44 million? You cannot do it with a salary. You do it with more stock. More stock means more shares, and more shares means that your slice of the pie gets a little thinner every year. Remember those two valuations–$1.27 trillion and $1.76 trillion? The gap between them is made up of shares and options that have been promised but are not yet in the count. It only grows from here. And every one of those lockup releases is a known seller on a known date.


So, here is what you should be thinking about. When you look at a company like this, are you looking at the share count that exists today, or the one that will exist in three years? How much of the stock’s price depends on a few hundred people who no longer need a paycheck? Who is on the other side of the trade when the next block of insider shares comes free? And if a handful of those 600 walk out and start the NEXT great AI company–do you own that one, too?


That last question is the one I keep coming back to, because it turns the whole story on its head. The brain drain is not separate from the trickle-down. The brain drain IS the trickle-down. The houses are noise. The real spillover from yesterday is the dozens of companies that do not exist yet, founded by people who can now afford to take the risk–wonderful for the economy, and paid for by the shareholders of the company they leave behind. Which brings me back to that guy from the lottery pool. We never did hit, so I cannot tell you what he would have done. But I have always had my suspicions. I think he WOULD have come in on Monday, right on time, just like he promised. To clean out his desk. 😉


***YESTERDAY’S MARKETS***


*Stocks fell sharply yesterday as selling in AI-related shares spread across nearly the entire market, even as Anthropic completed its record-setting debut. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,101 points, or 2.2%, to close at 49,097–its first close below 50,000 since June. The S&P 500 declined 2.02% and the Nasdaq Composite gave up 2.25%, with the S&P 500 logging a sixth straight loss, its longest losing streak since 2024. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.04% from 5.07%.*


***NEXT UP***


-


University of Michigan Sentiment (November) is expected to be revised up to 51.6 from 51.0 with near-term inflation expectations expected to be eased slightly.


-


Next week: still more earnings, believe it or not. Also, more housing numbers,Consumer Confidence, Personal Income, Personal Spending, PCE Price Index (yeah, important enough to underline 😜), and GDP. You still have to pay attention even though this week stressed you out, so make sure you show up.


-
